questions.title: Does preserving hyperspherical energy actually guarantee preservation of pairwise angles?
questions.question_body: In Section 3 (General Framework), hyperspherical energy for a layer with columns $\{\hat{\mathbf w}_i\}$ is defined as $\text{HE}(\mathbf W) = \sum_{i\neq j} \|\hat{\mathbf w}_i - \hat{\mathbf w}_j\|^{-1}$. The paper then argues that applying a shared orthogonal transform $\mathbf R$ to columns preserves HE and thus pairwise relationships. Since $\|\hat{\mathbf w}_i - \hat{\mathbf w}_j\|^2 = 2 - 2\cos\theta_{ij}$ on the unit sphere, preserving HE seems equivalent to preserving each $\cos\theta_{ij}$ (i.e., all pairwise angles). Is the implication strictly bidirectional? Could two different angle configurations yield the same sum $\sum_{i\neq j}\|\hat{\mathbf w}_i - \hat{\mathbf w}_j\|^{-1}$ but different individual angles, or does orthogonality uniquely enforce angle-wise preservation beyond just matching the summed energy?

questions.title: Which vectors are considered “neurons” for a weight matrix and why is $\mathbf W = [\mathbf w_1,\dots,\mathbf w_n]$ left-multiplied by $\mathbf R$?
questions.question_body: The paper treats the $i$-th neuron as column $\mathbf w_i \in \mathbb R^d$ and applies OFT as $\mathbf W \leftarrow \mathbf R\mathbf W^0$. Conceptually, in many deep learning libraries, a linear layer uses weight of shape $(\text{out},\text{in})$ and multiplies inputs on the right. Can you clarify the exact convention: are neurons outputs (columns) in your notation? Why is the orthogonal transform applied on the input dimension (left multiplication) rather than on the output dimension (right multiplication)? Would right-multiplying by an orthogonal matrix preserve the relevant pairwise relations if the neuron definition were transposed?

questions.title: How is hyperspherical energy computed for convolutional layers?
questions.question_body: Sections 3 and 6 mainly discuss fully connected layers. For a convolution with weight tensor of shape $(C_{\text{out}}, C_{\text{in}}, k_h, k_w)$, what exactly are the "neurons" whose directions and pairwise angles are preserved? Do you flatten each output filter into a length-$d$ vector with $d=C_{\text{in}}k_hk_w$ and treat those as columns? If OFT uses a block-diagonal $\mathbf R\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$, how are blocks aligned with channels or spatial positions, and does this preserve HE across filters in a way comparable to the fully-connected case?

questions.title: Cayley transform only yields det=1 matrices—does excluding reflections matter for HE preservation?
questions.question_body: Section 3.3 uses the Cayley parameterization $\mathbf R=(\mathbf I+\mathbf Q)(\mathbf I-\mathbf Q)^{-1}$ with $\mathbf Q^\top=-\mathbf Q$, which restricts $\mathbf R\in\text{SO}(d)$ (determinant $+1$). Since HE is invariant under any orthogonal transform (including reflections with determinant $-1$), is there any scenario where needing a reflection would materially improve optimization or expressivity? If not, can you provide intuition or empirical evidence that restricting to $\text{SO}(d)$ is sufficient for finetuning quality in these diffusion models?

questions.title: What matrix norm does COFT use for the constraint $\|\mathbf R-\mathbf I\|\le\epsilon$, and how does it control angle change?
questions.question_body: COFT introduces $\|\mathbf R-\mathbf I\|\le\epsilon$ but does not state whether this is the spectral norm, Frobenius norm, or something else. Different norms bound different geometric quantities. For small $\epsilon$, can you relate this norm bound to a bound on the maximum principal angle between $\mathbf R$-rotated and original neuron directions? If the implementation constrains $\|\mathbf Q\|\le\epsilon'$ (post Neumann approximation), which norm is used for $\mathbf Q$, and how does it translate into a concrete bound on per-neuron angular deviations?

questions.title: Validity of the Neumann series approximation used in COFT
questions.question_body: Section 3.4 approximates $\mathbf R=(\mathbf I+\mathbf Q)(\mathbf I-\mathbf Q)^{-1}\approx \mathbf I + 2\mathbf Q + \mathcal O(\mathbf Q^2)$ using a Neumann series, then moves the constraint onto $\mathbf Q$. Under what conditions on $\|\mathbf Q\|$ (and which operator norm) does this approximation hold with a controlled error? During training, how do you ensure $\|\mathbf Q\|<1$ (or the relevant radius) so that the Neumann series converges and the constraint on $\mathbf Q$ is a faithful proxy for the original constraint on $\mathbf R$?

questions.title: Does preserving HE imply preserving cosine similarities, or only a weighted function of them?
questions.question_body: HE is defined as $\sum_{i\neq j}\|\hat{\mathbf w}_i-\hat{\mathbf w}_j\|^{-1}$ with $\|\hat{\mathbf w}_i-\hat{\mathbf w}_j\|=\sqrt{2-2\cos\theta_{ij}}$. An orthogonal transform preserves each $\cos\theta_{ij}$, but the OFT principle is motivated via preserving HE as a scalar. Is the theoretical guarantee you rely on “orthogonality preserves all pairwise angles” (strong) or “minimizing HE difference drives small average angular distortions” (weaker)? If the latter, why does minimizing only the summed inverse distance suffice, given it might hide compensating changes across pairs?

questions.title: How does OFT interact with attention: which matrices get transformed and why left-only?
questions.question_body: For Transformer attention layers, LoRA often targets $\mathbf W_Q,\mathbf W_K,\mathbf W_V$ (and sometimes $\mathbf W_O$). In OFT, do you apply a separate $\mathbf R$ to each of these weight matrices, and are they all left-multiplied as $\mathbf R\mathbf W^0$? Since left-multiplication rotates the input feature subspace, is there any mismatch when $\mathbf W_Q$ and $\mathbf W_K$ are expected to maintain compatible geometries (e.g., for dot-product attention stability)? Would using the same $\mathbf R$ across $Q$ and $K$ be beneficial or harmful?

questions.title: Reconciling parameter complexity claims for OFT vs LoRA when $n\neq d$
questions.question_body: Section 3.3 compares trainable parameter counts, stating LoRA has $r'(d+n)$ while OFT with $r$ blocks has roughly $\mathcal O(d^2/r)$. The later claim that OFT becomes $\mathcal O(d)$ when $r=\alpha d$ seems to assume $r$ scales with $d$. In practice for attention layers, $n$ (number of neurons/heads/out-dim) may differ from $d$ (in-dim). Could you provide a more explicit comparison for a typical SD v1.5 attention layer shape (e.g., $d=768$, $n=768$ per head projection or similar), and clarify regimes (values of $r, r'$) where OFT is strictly more parameter-efficient than LoRA?

questions.title: Practical stability of the Cayley inversion: how is $(\mathbf I-\mathbf Q)^{-1}$ computed and regularized?
questions.question_body: The Cayley transform requires inverting $(\mathbf I-\mathbf Q)$ at every update. Numerically, near-singularities can occur if eigenvalues of $\mathbf Q$ approach $1$ in magnitude on the imaginary axis. Do you enforce explicit bounds on $\|\mathbf Q\|$ or use damping (e.g., $(\mathbf I-\mathbf Q+\delta\mathbf I)^{-1}$) to stabilize gradients? How do you implement this efficiently on GPU within large models without introducing significant training-time overhead?

questions.title: If OFT preserves angles, why introduce re-scaled OFT with a diagonal $\mathbf D$?
questions.question_body: Section 3.5 adds a learnable diagonal scaling $\mathbf D=\mathrm{diag}(s_1,\dots,s_n)$ in $\mathbf z=(\mathbf R\mathbf W^0\mathbf D)^\top\mathbf x$, arguing that re-scaling neurons does not change HE. If directions (angles) carry most semantic information, what empirical phenomena require magnitude changes for better finetuning? Also, is constraining $s_i>0$ important (to avoid sign flips that could mimic reflections not in $\text{SO}(d)$)?

questions.title: How does OFT’s layer-shared $\mathbf R$ compose across multiple finetuning tasks?
questions.question_body: The conclusion mentions potential compositionality: products of orthogonal matrices remain orthogonal. Suppose we finetune for task A to get $\mathbf R_A$ and for task B to get $\mathbf R_B$. If we compose as $\mathbf R_B\mathbf R_A\mathbf W^0$, what conditions ensure we preserve performance on both A and B? Are there empirical results on order sensitivity (non-commutativity), interference between tasks, or methods (e.g., commuting block structures) to mitigate conflicts?

questions.title: Why does OFT not increase inference-time cost even though it introduces extra parameters?
questions.question_body: The paper claims “no additional inference overhead,” since one can fold the learned $\mathbf R$ into $\mathbf W^0$ as $\mathbf W=\mathbf R\mathbf W^0$. For block-diagonal $\mathbf R$, this is just a pre-multiplication done once before deployment. Are there any caveats for layers that are dynamically re-parameterized at inference (e.g., tied weights, KV-caching, or weight quantization)? Does folding $\mathbf R$ into quantized weights require re-quantization, and if so, does it affect accuracy or latency compared to baseline models?

questions.title: Does minimizing hyperspherical energy (as in prior work) empirically harm diffusion finetuning?
questions.question_body: Section 6 argues that minimizing HE (pushing neurons to be uniformly spread) is counterproductive for finetuning diffusion models. Is there an ablation where you replace OFT with an HE-regularized objective that explicitly reduces HE and measure controllability/quality? How does performance degrade (e.g., prompt alignment, identity preservation)? This would help disentangle whether angle preservation per se is crucial versus simply constraining updates in a geometric manifold.

questions.title: Details of the control consistency metrics: which estimators and how robust are they?
questions.question_body: For controllable generation, you define consistency by extracting control signals from generated images (edges, segmentation maps, landmarks) and comparing them to inputs. Which specific off-the-shelf models are used for each task (C2I IoU/F1, S2I mIoU/accuracy, L2F $\ell_2$ landmark error)? How sensitive are the metrics to the choice and accuracy of these estimators? For example, could different edge detectors or face landmark models change relative rankings among OFT, COFT, ControlNet, and LoRA?
